about: Draft 'Today on WIOF' facts written by the WIOF team (Claude, 2026-11-05) for admins to check, source and mark reviewed. Applied by scripts/apply-occasion-facts.js as factStatus 'draft'. month is 1-12.

facts.fact: Veganuary began in the UK in 2014 as a pledge to try vegan eating for January, and well over a million people around the world have since signed up.
Regular moderate exercise, such as a brisk 30-minute walk on most days, is linked to better mood and lower stress as well as a healthier heart.
The US bald eagle was nearly wiped out by the pesticide DDT. After DDT was banned in 1972 it recovered, and it was taken off the endangered list in 2007.
Almost all of the roughly 18 penguin species live in the Southern Hemisphere; the Galápagos penguin is the only one that lives at the equator.
Red squirrels in Britain declined after grey squirrels were brought from North America in the 1800s: greys outcompete them and carry squirrelpox, which is deadly to reds.
Carbon dioxide in the air has risen from about 280 parts per million before the Industrial Revolution to more than 420 today, mainly from burning fossil fuels.
No two zebras have the same stripes: like a fingerprint, every zebra's pattern is unique.
World Wetlands Day marks the signing of the Ramsar Convention on wetlands in Ramsar, Iran, on 2 February 1971.
Pulses such as lentils, chickpeas and beans take nitrogen from the air and fix it in the soil, so they need less fertiliser and help the crops grown after them.
Bonobos live in the wild only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, south of the Congo River, and share about 98–99% of their DNA with humans.
Hippos spend most of the day in water to keep cool, and their skin gives off a reddish fluid that works like a natural sunscreen.
Pangolins are the only mammals covered in scales, made of keratin like our fingernails. Since 2017 all eight species have been protected from international commercial trade.
This day marks the first Rotary Club meeting, held in Chicago on 23 February 1905.
Polar bears hunt seals from sea ice, so shrinking Arctic ice is the biggest threat to them. Under their white fur, their skin is black.
UNAIDS launched Zero Discrimination Day in 2014 to promote equality before the law and in practice for everyone.
Adopting a rescue cat frees up shelter space for another animal, and neutering pets is one of the most effective ways to reduce the number of homeless animals.
World Wildlife Day falls on the day CITES, the treaty that regulates international trade in wild animals and plants, was signed in 1973.
Specific, sincere thanks matters: workplace studies consistently find that people who feel recognised are more engaged and less likely to leave.
Eating more plants and fewer animal products is one of the biggest ways a person can shrink the climate footprint of their diet.
The United Nations first celebrated International Women's Day on 8 March 1975, during International Women's Year.
About a year after stopping smoking, a person's extra risk of heart disease falls to about half that of someone who still smokes.

facts.occasion: International Day of Action for Rivers
facts.fact: Rivers, lakes and wetlands cover a tiny part of the planet yet are home to about one in ten known animal species, and freshwater wildlife is declining faster than wildlife on land or at sea.
Social workers support people through some of life's hardest moments, from child protection to disaster relief; the day is promoted by the International Federation of Social Workers.
Giant pandas eat mostly bamboo, many kilograms of it a day. Thanks to conservation work in China, the IUCN moved them from Endangered to Vulnerable in 2016.
Most adults need at least 7 hours of sleep a night; regularly sleeping less is linked to heart disease, diabetes and low mood.
World Sparrow Day was started in 2010 by the Nature Forever Society in India. Nest boxes and native plants that attract insects for chicks help house sparrows return to cities.
The UN declared the International Day of Happiness in 2012 at the initiative of Bhutan, which measures progress by Gross National Happiness.
Forests cover about 31% of the world's land and are home to most of the animals and plants that live on land.
Only about 2.5% of the water on Earth is fresh, and most of that is frozen in ice and glaciers. World Water Day has been held every year since 1993.
World Meteorological Day marks the founding of the World Meteorological Organization, whose convention came into force on 23 March 1950.
Manatees are gentle plant-eaters that can eat about a tenth of their body weight in plants a day; collisions with boats are one of their biggest threats.
Rats are clever and social. Trained African giant pouched rats sniff out landmines and tuberculosis, helping make land safe again.
World Health Day marks the founding of the World Health Organization, whose constitution came into force on 7 April 1948.
Plants make the oxygen we breathe and are the start of almost every food chain; more than 80% of the food people eat comes from plants.
Microvolunteering means small, quick acts of help, such as mapping, transcribing or a few minutes online, that add up when many people take part.
Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly. Many eat huge numbers of insects every night, and others pollinate plants such as agave.
The first Earth Day, on 22 April 1970, brought about 20 million Americans out to call for environmental protection; today it is marked in nearly 200 countries.
Scientists are guided by the '3Rs': Replace animal tests where possible, Reduce the number of animals used, and Refine methods to cause less suffering.
World Penguin Day is timed with the yearly northward migration of Adélie penguins in Antarctica.
World Veterinary Day is promoted by the World Veterinary Association. Vets protect people too, since many human diseases come from animals.
Only five rhino species are left, and three of them, the Javan, Sumatran and black rhino, are critically endangered, mainly because of poaching for their horn.
Chickens descend from the red junglefowl of Southeast Asia, and they can recognise many individual faces in their flock.
Donkeys were domesticated in Africa thousands of years ago and still carry water and loads for millions of families today.
The Arctic tern makes the longest migration of any animal, flying between the Arctic and the Antarctic every year.
The IUCN Red List has assessed more than 160,000 species, and over 45,000 of them are threatened with extinction.
The UN marks World Bee Day on 20 May, the birthday of Anton Janša, a Slovenian pioneer of modern beekeeping. Bees and other pollinators help produce about a third of the food we eat.
The International Day for Biological Diversity marks the adoption of the text of the Convention on Biological Diversity on 22 May 1992.
Turtles have been around for more than 200 million years, since the age of the early dinosaurs; six of the seven sea turtle species are threatened.
Sea otters have the densest fur of any animal, up to about a million hairs per square inch, which keeps them warm without a layer of blubber.
Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor but support about a quarter of all marine species.
The UN declared 3 June World Bicycle Day in 2018. Cycling short trips instead of driving cuts air pollution and is good for the heart.

facts.occasion: International Day of Innocent Children Victims of Aggression
facts.fact: The UN General Assembly set up this day in 1982 to recognise the pain suffered by children who are victims of physical, mental and emotional abuse.
The UN set up World Environment Day at the 1972 Stockholm Conference on the Human Environment, and it has been held every year since 1973.
The WHO estimates that almost 1 in 10 people in the world fall ill every year from eating contaminated food.
The ocean produces at least half of the oxygen we breathe, much of it from tiny plankton, and absorbs about a quarter of the carbon dioxide people release.
The Iberian lynx was once one of the most endangered cats on Earth, with fewer than 100 left in 2002; conservation work has since brought its numbers to well over 1,000.
The International Labour Organization launched this day in 2002. Around 160 million children worldwide are in child labour.
A single modern wind turbine can make enough electricity in a year for hundreds to thousands of homes, without burning any fuel.
World Refill Day encourages refilling bottles and containers instead of buying single-use plastic; one reusable bottle can replace hundreds of plastic ones a year.

facts.occasion: World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought
facts.fact: The UN Convention to Combat Desertification was adopted on 17 June 1994. Restoring damaged land helps it hold water, store carbon and grow food.
The wandering albatross has the largest wingspan of any living bird, up to about 3.5 metres, and can glide for hours without flapping its wings.
World Refugee Day was first held in 2001, the 50th anniversary of the 1951 Refugee Convention.
The UN declared the International Day of Yoga in 2014 on India's proposal; 21 June was chosen because it is the longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere.
A camel's hump stores fat, not water, and a thirsty camel can drink more than 100 litres of water in a few minutes.
The tropics are home to about 80% of the world's land species, and by 2050 around half of the world's people are expected to live there.
A plastic bag is often used for minutes but can last for centuries; well over 100 countries now ban or tax single-use plastic bags.
World Population Day began in 1989, inspired by the 'Day of Five Billion' in 1987. The world passed 8 billion people in November 2022.
Margaret Knight invented a machine to make flat-bottomed paper bags in the 1870s. Whatever the material, reusing a bag many times matters most.
World Chimpanzee Day marks the day in 1960 when Jane Goodall began studying wild chimpanzees in Gombe, Tanzania.
Most snakes are harmless to people, and many help farmers by eating rats and mice that damage crops.
The last ten years were the warmest on record, and the world is now well over 1°C warmer than in the late 1800s.
More than half of the world's economic output depends moderately or highly on nature, through things like clean water, fertile soil and pollination.
International Tiger Day was agreed at the 2010 St Petersburg Tiger Summit; India is now home to about three quarters of the world's wild tigers.
World Ranger Day honours the rangers who protect wildlife and wild places, on the founding anniversary of the International Ranger Federation in 1992.
For its size, the clouded leopard has the longest canine teeth of any living cat, and it can climb down trees head first.
India's National Handloom Day remembers the Swadeshi Movement launched on 7 August 1905; handloom weaving is one of the country's largest rural livelihoods after farming.
International Cat Day was started in 2002 by the International Fund for Animal Welfare.

facts.occasion: International Day of the World's Indigenous Peoples
facts.fact: Indigenous peoples are about 6% of the world's population but care for lands that hold much of the world's remaining biodiversity.
Africa's wild lions have declined sharply in recent decades, and the only wild Asiatic lions live in and around Gir Forest in Gujarat, India.
Elephants are 'ecosystem engineers': they dig for water, open up paths through forests and spread seeds far and wide in their dung.
Wolves were brought back to Yellowstone National Park in 1995, and they are widely credited with changing how elk graze, which helped trees and riverbanks recover.
World Humanitarian Day remembers the 2003 bombing of the UN headquarters in Baghdad, in which 22 people were killed, including UN envoy Sérgio Vieira de Mello.

facts.occasion: International Day for the Remembrance of Slave Trade and Abolition
facts.fact: UNESCO chose 23 August because on the night of 22–23 August 1791 an uprising began in Saint-Domingue, now Haiti, that helped bring about the end of the transatlantic slave trade.
Dogs were the first animals people domesticated, at least 15,000 years ago, long before farming began.
Japan Dolphin Day draws attention to the dolphin drive hunts in Taiji, Japan, which usually begin each September.
World Coconut Day marks the founding of the Asian and Pacific Coconut Community in 1969; nearly every part of the coconut palm is used, from food and oil to fibre and timber.
Vultures clean up carcasses and stop diseases from spreading. In South Asia their numbers crashed by over 95% after cattle were treated with the painkiller diclofenac, which is deadly to them.
The UN chose 5 September, the anniversary of Mother Teresa's death in 1997, for the International Day of Charity.
The Montreal Protocol, signed on 16 September 1987, phased out most of the chemicals damaging the ozone layer, which is now on track to heal within a few decades.
Red pandas aren't close relatives of giant pandas: they belong to a family of their own, although they also eat mostly bamboo.
Some bamboo species can grow almost a metre in a single day, making bamboo one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth.
Zero Emissions Day, first held in 2008, asks people to use as little fossil fuel as they can for one day.
WWF South Africa announced World Rhino Day in 2010. Southern white rhinos were brought back from fewer than 100 animals in the late 1800s to thousands today.
World Gorilla Day marks the founding of Dian Fossey's Karisoke Research Center in Rwanda on 24 September 1967; mountain gorillas have since grown to more than 1,000.
World Rivers Day is held on the fourth Sunday of September; it grew out of BC Rivers Day, started in Canada in 1980 by Mark Angelo.
The cassowary of northern Australia and New Guinea is one of the heaviest birds in the world and swallows fruit whole, spreading the seeds of many rainforest trees.
28 September is the anniversary of the death of Louis Pasteur, who developed the first rabies vaccine. Vaccinating dogs is the best way to protect people from rabies.
World Vegetarian Day was established by the North American Vegetarian Society in 1977.
The UN set up World Habitat Day, held on the first Monday of October, to reflect on everyone's right to adequate shelter.
4 October is the feast day of St Francis of Assisi, the patron saint of animals, which is why World Animal Day is held on this date.
India marks Wildlife Week from 2 to 8 October each year; the country is home to around 7–8% of all recorded species.
Badgers live in family groups in underground setts, which can be used by generation after generation of badgers for decades.
World Mental Health Day was first held in 1992. About one in eight people worldwide lives with a mental health condition.

facts.occasion: International Day of the Girl Child
facts.fact: The UN declared 11 October the International Day of the Girl Child in 2011, and it was first celebrated in 2012.
Early warnings save lives: warning people just 24 hours before a storm or heatwave can cut the damage it causes by about 30%.
The UN first observed the International Day of Rural Women in 2008. Rural women grow much of the world's food, often with less access to land, credit and training.
World Food Day marks the founding of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization on 16 October 1945. Roughly a third of all food produced is lost or wasted.
The okapi has zebra-like stripes but is the giraffe's only living relative, and it is found in the wild only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Sloths move so slowly that algae grow in their fur, giving them a greenish tint that helps them hide in the trees.
Wombats are the only animals known to produce cube-shaped droppings, which they leave on rocks and logs to mark their territory.
Snow leopards live high in the mountains of Central and South Asia, including the Indian Himalaya, and use their long, thick tails for balance and warmth.
River dolphins live in some of the world's great rivers, including the Ganges, Indus and Amazon; the Ganges river dolphin is India's national aquatic animal.
Lemurs live in the wild only on Madagascar, and they are among the most threatened groups of mammals on Earth.
World Vegan Day marks the founding of The Vegan Society in the UK in November 1944, when the word 'vegan' was coined.
Jellyfish have no brain, heart or bones, and they have drifted through the oceans for more than 500 million years.
The numbat, a small marsupial from Western Australia, eats almost nothing but termites, up to about 20,000 a day.
Even 5 to 10 minutes of running a day, at a slow pace, is linked to a lower risk of dying from heart disease.

facts.occasion: World Day to Protect the Environemnt in War
facts.fact: In 2001 the UN declared 6 November the International Day for Preventing the Exploitation of the Environment in War and Armed Conflict.
The numbat, a small marsupial from Western Australia, eats almost nothing but termites, up to about 20,000 a day.
November is Manatee Awareness Month in Florida, when manatees move to warmer waters such as natural springs for the winter.

facts.occasion: World Science Day for Peace and Development
facts.fact: UNESCO proclaimed World Science Day for Peace and Development in 2001, and it was first celebrated on 10 November 2002.
World Kindness Day was introduced in 1998 by the World Kindness Movement; studies suggest small acts of kindness lift the giver's wellbeing too.
UNESCO adopted its Declaration of Principles on Tolerance on 16 November 1995, the UN's Year for Tolerance.

facts.occasion: International Day of Elimination of Violence against Men
facts.fact: Worldwide, men die by suicide at more than twice the rate of women, so talking openly about mental health and asking for help matters.
International Men's Day, marked on 19 November since 1999, focuses on men's health and wellbeing; worldwide, men die by suicide at more than twice the rate of women.
World Fisheries Day is celebrated by fishing communities around the world; more than a third of the world's fish stocks are now fished at unsustainable levels.

facts.occasion: International Day of Elimination of Violence against Women
facts.fact: The UN chose 25 November to honour the Mirabal sisters, political activists killed in the Dominican Republic on that day in 1960.
The jaguar is the largest cat in the Americas and has one of the strongest bites of any big cat, strong enough to crack turtle shells.
India's National Pollution Prevention Day on 2 December remembers the victims of the 1984 Bhopal gas tragedy, one of the worst industrial disasters in history.
The cheetah, the fastest land animal, was brought back to India in 2022, seventy years after it was declared extinct there.
It can take up to a thousand years to form just a few centimetres of topsoil, and about 95% of our food comes directly or indirectly from soil.
International Animal Rights Day is held on 10 December, Human Rights Day, to call for the rights of animals to be respected too.
Mountains supply much of the world's fresh water, and the UN has marked International Mountain Day every year since 2003.
Monkey Day began in 2000 as a joke between two art students in Michigan and is now used to raise awareness of threats to monkeys and other primates.
The Universal Hour of Peace runs from 11:30 pm on 31 December to 12:30 am on 1 January, inviting people to begin the new year with peaceful thoughts and actions.
